title: lateinit, lazy, casts, numbers
scopeHtml: Scope: lateinit vs lazy vs nullable, lateinit internals and restrictions, is/as/as?, boxing and the Integer cache, numeric conversions, Char/String internals, type inference limits, and reflection-based parsers that break Kotlin null-safety. (Lazy thread-safety modes and Android property delegates are covered in the properties & delegation section.)

questions.promptHtml: You have a property that can't be given a value in the constructor. When do you pick lateinit var, by lazy, or a nullable var x: T? = null?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you choose based on who initializes the value and when, rather than habit. It also shows whether you understand what failure each option produces.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I start by asking who supplies the value. If something outside the class supplies it later, through an injector, a lifecycle callback or a test setup, I use lateinit var. I'm promising it gets set before first read, and if I break that promise I get a loud UninitializedPropertyAccessException. If the class can compute the value itself but it's costly or not always needed, I use val by lazy: it computes once on first read and caches. If "no value" is a real, valid state, such as no logged-in user or a view that was destroyed, I use a nullable type, so the compiler makes every caller handle it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The three options say different things about how the property behaves over time:

lateinit var val by lazy {} var x: T? = null
Who initializes External code, any time The property itself, on first get Anyone
Mutable Yes (var only) No (val only) Yes
Can it be "absent" again No (no un-set from Kotlin) No Yes, assign null
Read before init Throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException Runs the initializer Returns null; compiler forces handling
Types allowed Non-null, non-primitive Any Any
Runtime cost One field + null check in getter Delegate object + lambda object + (default) lock One field
Thread safety None SYNCHRONIZED by default None

How to decide:

  • The value has a known source at declaration time → lazy. The initializer is part of the declaration, so it can never be forgotten.
  • The value comes from outside, after construction (field injection with @Inject lateinit var, onCreate, @Before in tests) → lateinit. Using a nullable here pushes !! or ?. onto every access even though the value is always present once the class is running.
  • Absence is part of the domain → nullable. A lateinit that you "reset" by setting a dummy value, or that you guard with isInitialized everywhere, is really a nullable property in disguise.

A lazy lambda can capture this, so it can reach other members. That makes it a good fit for derived values (val formatter by lazy { DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(pattern, locale) }). It is a bad fit for anything tied to a lifecycle that ends before the owner does, because the cached value outlives that lifecycle. The Fragment-view case is in the delegation section.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: CartRepository
) : ViewModel() {
    // Derived, costly, always computable by the class itself -> lazy
    private val priceFormatter by lazy { NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.getDefault()) }

    // "No coupon" is a real state -> nullable
    var appliedCoupon: Coupon? = null
        private set
}

class CheckoutFragment : Fragment() {
    // Set by the framework/injector after construction -> lateinit
    @Inject lateinit var analytics: Analytics
}

// Broken: nullable used for an always-present dependency -> !! everywhere
class BadFragment : Fragment() {
    var analytics: Analytics? = null
    fun track() = analytics!!.log("x") // the NPE moves around instead of failing fast at the source
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using lateinit for state that really can be absent, then scattering if (::x.isInitialized) checks around.
  • Using lazy on a var. That doesn't compile, because lazy gives a read-only delegate.
  • Assuming lateinit is thread-safe. It is a plain field, with no publication guarantees across threads.
  • Holding a lifecycle-scoped object such as a View, Context or binding in lazy on a longer-lived owner. The cached value leaks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can lazy be reset? → No. The stdlib Lazy has no reset. If you need resettable caching, write a small holder yourself or use a nullable field with a getter that fills it.
  2. What does lazy cost compared with lateinit? → A Lazy object, the lambda object, and a lock object for SYNCHRONIZED mode, plus a volatile read on every access. lateinit is just a field and a null check. The difference only matters in hot paths or on objects you create in very large numbers.
  3. Which would you use for a dependency in a class you control? → Neither. I'd use constructor injection with a private val. lateinit is for classes the framework instantiates (Activities, Fragments, Services) where you can't own the constructor.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer stops at "lateinit is var, lazy is val". A senior answer explains the choice in terms of who owns initialization and which failure you want: a loud crash at the source, guaranteed initialization, or forced null-handling. They also point out that constructor injection removes most uses of lateinit.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that turned every lateinit into T? "to be safe" swapped one clear crash for dozens of !! NPEs that fired far from the real cause, and their crash-group count went up.

questions.promptHtml: What does a lateinit var compile to on the JVM, and what exactly happens when you read one that hasn't been set?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can reason at the bytecode level, and whether you know how lateinit behaves from Java and from DI frameworks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A lateinit var compiles to a normal nullable JVM reference field, with null meaning "not set yet". The getter checks that field. If it's null, the getter calls Intrinsics.throwUninitializedPropertyAccessException with the property name, which throws kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property x has not been initialized. The setter has no check. One unusual detail: the backing field is exposed to Java with the same visibility as the property's setter. That is what lets Dagger/Hilt write @Inject lateinit var fields directly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decompiled shape (simplified) for class A { lateinit var name: String }:

public final class A {
    public String name;                       // field visibility == setter visibility

    public final String getName() {
        String v = this.name;
        if (v != null) return v;
        Intrinsics.throwUninitializedPropertyAccessException("name");
        return null; // unreachable
    }

    public final void setName(String v) {
        Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter(v, "<set-?>");   // can't set null from Java either
        this.name = v;
    }
}

What follows from this:

  1. The check runs on every access through the getter. Inside the class, Kotlin still reads through the accessor logic, so even internal reads are checked. The check is one compare plus a branch the CPU predicts well, so it costs almost nothing.
  2. Setting null is rejected by the generated parameter null check, which throws NullPointerException in Kotlin 1.4+.
  3. The field is visible to Java. Java code can read a.name directly, skip the check, and get null. Java or reflection can also write null straight into the field. That is how a lateinit can end up "un-initialized again".
  4. Annotations such as @Inject on a lateinit property are placed on the field by default, which is what Dagger needs. That is the reason lateinit exists in Android code at all.
  5. lateinit is allowed on member properties, and since Kotlin 1.2 also on top-level properties and local variables. A local lateinit var is checked when it is read.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Session {
    lateinit var token: String

    fun header(): String = "Bearer $token"   // throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException if unset
}

fun main() {
    val s = Session()
    runCatching { s.header() }
        .onFailure { println(it) } // kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property token has not been initialized
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the exception is an NPE. It isn't: UninitializedPropertyAccessException extends RuntimeException, so Crashlytics groups it separately and the property name appears in the message.
  • Assuming a private lateinit is truly private to Java. The field is private only if the setter is private, which a private property's setter is. With lateinit var x; private set, the field is private too.
  • Expecting lateinit to give memory visibility across threads. Without @Volatile or another happens-before edge, a thread can see a stale null and throw.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why expose the field at all? → So that injection frameworks and Java code can set it without going through Kotlin accessors. Field injection was the original motivation.
  2. Can you put @Volatile on a lateinit? → Yes, @Volatile lateinit var compiles and makes the field volatile. It fixes visibility but not check-then-act races.
  3. What does lateinit look like after R8? → R8 usually inlines the getter, so you get a field load, a null check and a call to the throw helper. The property name string stays in the message even when the field name is obfuscated, which helps when reading a crash.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer says "it throws if you access it early". A senior answer describes the null-sentinel field, the exception type and its message, the setter-visibility field exposure, and how Java or reflection can bypass the check.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Crash dashboards often show UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property binding has not been initialized. Because the property name is in the message, it is one of the easiest crash groups to triage, as long as nobody wraps it in a generic catch.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't lateinit be used with Int, with nullable types, with val, or with custom getters? What do you use instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Each restriction follows directly from how lateinit is implemented. Candidates who explain the mechanism instead of memorizing the rules stand out.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every restriction comes from one design choice: lateinit uses null in the backing field to mean "not set". A primitive int field can't hold null, so Int, Long, Boolean and the other primitives are out. A nullable type would make null mean both "not set" and "set to null", so that is banned too. val is banned because the whole point is to assign the value after construction. Custom accessors are banned because the compiler generates the getter that does the check. For primitives I use Delegates.notNull<Int>(), or I rethink the design and use a nullable or a default value.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Restriction Reason
Not on primitive types (Int, Double, Boolean...) They compile to JVM primitives, which have no null. Boxing them would quietly change the field type and its cost.
Not on nullable types null is already taken as the "uninitialized" marker, so the two meanings would clash.
Only var You must be able to assign it after construction.
No custom getter/setter The compiler owns the getter because that is where the check lives.
Not in the primary constructor A constructor parameter is initialized by definition.
Type must not be an inline/value class over a primitive or nullable Same null-representation problem. The exact rules depend on the underlying type, so check your Kotlin version's diagnostics.

Alternatives:

  • var count: Int by Delegates.notNull(). It stores the value in a delegate object, and reading before setting throws IllegalStateException("Property count should be initialized before get."). The cost is one extra object per property plus a virtual call per access.
  • A sensible default (var retryCount = 0), if 0 is semantically fine.
  • A nullable Int?, if "not set" is meaningful. Accept the boxing.
  • Restructure so the value arrives through the constructor.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import kotlin.properties.Delegates

class Player {
    // lateinit var volume: Int          // compile error: 'lateinit' modifier is not allowed on properties of primitive types
    var volume: Int by Delegates.notNull()

    // lateinit var nickname: String?    // compile error: not allowed on nullable types
    var nickname: String? = null
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Switching to Int? "because lateinit doesn't work". Every read then pays for boxing and unboxing, and callers must handle null.
  • Putting Delegates.notNull() on hot properties of objects created in large numbers. That adds one extra object per property per instance.
  • Assuming lateinit var s: String accepts "" as "unset". It doesn't: any non-null value counts as initialized.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Delegates.notNull() support isInitialized? → No. ::x.isInitialized only works on lateinit properties. With notNull you'd have to catch the exception or track state yourself.
  2. Can a lateinit have a generic type T? → Yes, if T is non-null (T : Any). With an unbounded T, the compiler rejects it because T could be nullable.
  3. Why not let lateinit Int box under the hood? → It would silently change the field type and its performance, and it would break the "field is exposed to Java" contract for something that looks like an int. The language designers chose an explicit error instead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer lists the rules. A senior answer derives all of them from the null-sentinel design and picks the alternative based on semantics and cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An Int? "ID not loaded yet" field read in a scroll listener boxed on every frame. Changing it to a plain Int with -1 documented as a sentinel removed the allocations seen in Memory Profiler.

questions.promptHtml: How does ::x.isInitialized work, where can you call it, and why do some reviewers treat it as a code smell?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It looks like a small API, but the answer reveals lexical-scope rules, how the compiler intrinsifies it, and design judgment.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: this::x.isInitialized (available since Kotlin 1.2) returns whether the lateinit backing field is non-null. The compiler doesn't use reflection for it. It compiles straight to a null check on the field. That's why you can only call it where the backing field is lexically accessible: inside the declaring class, an outer class, or the same file for top-level properties. I treat frequent use as a smell, because a lateinit that needs checking is usually a nullable value in disguise.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Syntax: ::prop.isInitialized for top-level or local scope, this::prop.isInitialized for a member, and other::prop.isInitialized for a bound reference, which is still subject to access rules.
  • Compilation: the property-reference expression is replaced with this.prop != null on the raw field. No KProperty object is created and no kotlin-reflect is needed.
  • Access rule: the compiler reports an error ("Backing field of 'var x: String' is not accessible at this point") when you call it from a subclass in another file, from an extension function, or from another class. In each of those places the field is out of reach.
  • There is no inverse: Kotlin can't "uninitialize" a lateinit. Tear-down code therefore can't reset it, and the property stays pinned to the last value until the owner is garbage-collected.

Legitimate uses:

  • Idempotent cleanup: if (::player.isInitialized) player.release() in onDestroy, where creation was conditional.
  • Test teardown, when setup may have failed partway.

Smell indicators: the same property is checked in more than one or two places, it's checked in a getter, or a separate "isReady" flag duplicates it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class VideoActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private lateinit var player: ExoPlayer

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        if (intent.hasExtra("url")) {
            player = ExoPlayer.Builder(this).build()
        }
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        if (this::player.isInitialized) player.release()   // OK: idempotent cleanup
        super.onDestroy()
    }
}

open class Base { lateinit var dep: String }
class Child : Base() {
    // fun check() = this::dep.isInitialized   // compile error: backing field not accessible here
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting it to work from a subclass or an extension. It doesn't. Expose a protected val isDepReady get() = ::dep.isInitialized from the base class if you really need it.
  • Using it to build a "check-then-init" lazy by hand on multiple threads. That is a race. Use lazy instead.
  • Writing ::x.isInitialized and forgetting the this qualifier on a member in an ambiguous context. It's usually fine, but this:: makes the intent clear.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it allocate a KProperty? → No. It is an intrinsic that compiles to a field null check.
  2. How would you release a lateinit to let GC collect it? → You can't through Kotlin. Make it nullable, or release the resource while keeping the reference (the owner's own lifetime then decides when it is collected).
  3. Is it thread-safe? → It's a plain field read. Without @Volatile it can return a stale false on another thread.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer says "it checks if lateinit was set". A senior answer explains the field-access intrinsic, the lexical restriction and its error, the lack of a reset, and when the check shows the property should be nullable.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Paired isInitialized checks spread across 9 call sites in a media screen kept out-of-date state alive across re-entries. Converting the property to a nullable with a single owner removed a class of "released player reused" crashes.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping app has 2M DAU. A week after release 7.4, Crashlytics shows a new top crash at 0.35% of sessions:

Fatal Exception: kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property cartPresenter has not been initialized
    at com.shop.MainActivity.getCartPresenter(MainActivity.kt:41)
    at com.shop.cart.CartBadgeFragment.onCreate(CartBadgeFragment.kt:28)
    at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.performCreate(Fragment.java:3094)
    ...
    at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentActivity.onCreate(FragmentActivity.java:...)
    at com.shop.MainActivity.onCreate(MainActivity.kt:55)

MainActivity.onCreate calls super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) on line 55 and assigns cartPresenter = CartPresenter(...) on line 58. CartBadgeFragment.onCreate does (requireActivity() as MainActivity).cartPresenter.attach(this). QA can't reproduce it on fresh launches. 80% of crashes come from devices with 3 GB of RAM or less. The release also bumped the Firebase SDK.
questions.promptHtml: What's going on, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in if (::cartPresenter.isInitialized)", or "make it nullable and use ?.". Either one hides the crash, and the badge silently never attaches. Blaming the Firebase SDK because the release bumped it is the red herring.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does savedInstanceState tend to be non-null in the crashing sessions? Custom keys or breadcrumbs would show this, and it points straight at process-death restore.
    • When did CartBadgeFragment start reading cartPresenter in onCreate? Let's diff 7.3 against 7.4.
    • Are the crashes clustered on cold starts from recents? Process-state logs would show it.
    • Is the Firebase bump touching activity lifecycle at all? I want to rule it out quickly.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that moves the cartPresenter assignment to before super.onCreate if it doesn't depend on restored state. Or roll back the badge fragment's onCreate access through remote config, if a flag exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Process-death restore order. When the system recreates the Activity, super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) restores the FragmentManager, and restored fragments run onAttach/onCreate inside that call, before line 58. Low-RAM devices get process kills more often, which matches the device split. On a fresh launch, the fragment is added later, so the bug is invisible.
    2. Configuration change. This is the same mechanism, but it would also show up on high-RAM devices with rotation. It's less likely given the RAM skew.
    3. Firebase SDK. Nothing in the stack trace comes from it, so it's a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: I'd turn on Developer options → "Don't keep activities", or run adb shell am kill com.shop while the app is in the background and then reopen it from recents. That reproduces the crash deterministically. Breakpoints in MainActivity.onCreate and CartBadgeFragment.onCreate show the fragment's method running inside super.onCreate. A savedInstanceState != null custom key in Crashlytics confirms it in the field.
  5. Root cause: The fragment pulls a dependency from its host Activity in onCreate. During restore, fragment callbacks are dispatched from inside FragmentActivity.onCreate, so the host's lateinit isn't assigned yet. lateinit did its job: it failed loudly at the right place.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: assign the presenter before super.onCreate, if it doesn't need restored fragments or Activity state.
    • Long-term: remove the dependency on the host entirely. Put CartPresenter behind DI or a shared activityViewModels() ViewModel, which is created on demand and survives configuration changes:
    class CartBadgeFragment : Fragment(R.layout.cart_badge) {
    private val cartVm: CartViewModel by activityViewModels()

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                cartVm.count.collect { view.findViewById<TextView>(R.id.badge).text = "$it" }
            }
        }
    }
}
  7. Prevention: Run a "Don't keep activities" pass in the QA regression checklist. Add an instrumentation test that uses ActivityScenario.recreate(). Add a lint or review rule that forbids requireActivity() as SomeActivity dependency pulls in onAttach/onCreate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't add isInitialized guards: the badge would silently stay broken and the crash would just move elsewhere. I also wouldn't make the presenter nullable with ?.attach, for the same reason. The ordering dependency is the bug, not the lateinit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why not just move the line before super.onCreate?" → That works only if the presenter doesn't need anything super.onCreate sets up, such as restored ViewModels or the fragment manager. It is fragile, because the next dependency added to the presenter breaks it again.
  • "Would Hilt fix this?" → Yes for this crash. The generated Hilt_MainActivity injects at the very start of the onCreate chain. In recent versions it does this through an OnContextAvailableListener, which ComponentActivity.onCreate dispatches before FragmentActivity dispatches fragment onCreate. So @Inject lateinit var fields are already set when restored fragments run. Assignments in your own onCreate after super are not.
  • "How do you get the savedInstanceState signal into Crashlytics cheaply?" → setCustomKey("restored", savedInstanceState != null) in onCreate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team in this position "fixed" a similar crash with null checks, and checkout conversion dropped about 1% because a restored screen showed a stale cart. Reproducing it with "Don't keep activities" found the real ordering bug in 10 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests try/catch, isInitialized or nullable without explaining why it crashes. Blames the SDK.
  • Hire: Identifies process-death restore and the fragment-callbacks-inside-super.onCreate ordering, and reproduces it with "Don't keep activities".
  • Strong hire: All of the above, plus explains why low-RAM devices dominate, removes the fragment-to-activity coupling with a ViewModel or DI, adds recreate tests, and explains why Hilt injects before super.onCreate.

questions.promptHtml: Explain is, as, and as? in Kotlin. What does each do at runtime, and when would you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These are basic tools, but how you use them shows your error-handling habits and whether you rely on smart casts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: is is a runtime type check that returns a Boolean. After it succeeds on a stable value, the compiler smart-casts the value, so I don't need an explicit cast. as is an unsafe cast: if the value isn't that type it throws ClassCastException, and casting null to a non-null type throws NullPointerException since Kotlin 1.4. as? is the safe cast: it returns null on mismatch. I usually pair it with ?: to supply a default or return early. I use when (x) { is A -> ... } for branching on types, as? at trust boundaries, and as only when a mismatch really is a programmer error and I want it to crash.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
On the JVM:

  • x is String → instanceof String.
  • x as String → checkcast String. If x is null and the target is non-null, Kotlin first emits an explicit null check, because checkcast lets null through on the JVM.
  • x as String? → a plain checkcast, which lets null through.
  • x as? String → instanceof and then either the value or null.
Expression x = "a" x = 1 x = null
x is String true false false
x as String "a" ClassCastException NullPointerException (1.4+)
x as String? "a" ClassCastException null
x as? String "a" null null

as? gives a nullable result, so x as? String has type String?. Writing (x as? String)!! is just as with a worse error message.

Generic types are checked only up to their class, because of erasure. That is covered in the generics section and in the next question.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun describe(x: Any?): String = when (x) {
    is String -> "string of ${x.length}"        // smart cast, no 'as'
    is Int    -> "int ${x + 1}"
    null      -> "null"
    else      -> "other ${x::class.simpleName}"
}

fun parseArgs(args: Bundle) {
    // Trust boundary: data may be malformed -> as? with a fallback
    val count = args.get("count") as? Int ?: 0
}

// Programmer error should crash loudly -> as
val host = requireActivity() as HostActivity

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing if (x is String) { (x as String).length }. The cast is redundant noise.
  • Using as? and then ignoring the null. That turns a bug into silent data loss.
  • Expecting as with a nullable source to throw a ClassCastException for null. Kotlin 1.4+ throws NullPointerException ("null cannot be cast to non-null type kotlin.String").
  • !is combined with an early return is the idiomatic guard: if (x !is Foo) return.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When does is fail to smart-cast? → On mutable or open properties, custom getters, and properties from other modules. The compiler can't prove the value didn't change (see the smart-cast question in the type-system section).
  2. Is as free when the static type already matches? → The compiler removes upcasts and warns "No cast needed".
  3. How do you check x is List<String>? → You can't. Erasure means you write x is List<*> and check the elements yourself.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer gives the definitions. A senior answer maps each to bytecode (instanceof/checkcast), knows the null-cast exception type, and has a policy: crash on programmer errors, as? with handling at trust boundaries, and when/smart casts everywhere else.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sweep that replaced as with as? in deep-link parsing turned ClassCastException crashes into silently broken links. Fallbacks plus a logged non-fatal gave visibility without crashes.

questions.promptHtml: What is an unchecked cast in Kotlin? Why can a bad cast throw ClassCastException somewhere other than where you wrote as?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This separates people who've actually debugged heap pollution from people who just suppress warnings. It's at the boundary between casts and erasure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When you cast to a generic type such as as List<String>, or as T inside a generic function, the JVM can only check the raw class, or nothing at all for T. So the compiler warns "Unchecked cast" and emits little or no check. The wrong value passes through, and the ClassCastException appears later. It appears wherever the compiler inserted a concrete checkcast, which is usually where you first read an element as String. I treat every @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") as a debt that needs a justification comment. I prefer reified type parameters or explicit element checks.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Erasure means List<String> and List<Int> are the same java.util.List at runtime. So:

val raw: Any = listOf(1, 2, 3)
val strings = raw as List<String>      // checkcast java/util/List -> passes
...                                    // value travels through 5 layers
val first: String = strings[0]         // compiler inserts checkcast String here -> ClassCastException

This is heap pollution: a variable whose static type is wrong about its runtime contents. The stack trace points at the read site, maybe in a different module or thread, not at the bad cast.

In a generic function fun <T> unsafe(x: Any?): T = x as T, there is no checkcast at all inside the function, because T erases to Any?. The check happens at the call site, where T is concrete, and only if the result is used as that type.

reified fixes the single-level case: inline fun <reified T> Any?.castOrNull(): T? = this as? T really checks T's class at the inlined site. It still can't check nested arguments: castOrNull<List<String>>() only checks List.

Null casts: null as String → NPE. null as T in a generic function where T is inferred non-null → no failure there, and the NPE appears at the first use. That is another failure that surfaces somewhere else.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
fun <T> Bundle.unsafeGet(key: String): T = get(key) as T   // no runtime check at all

fun demo(b: Bundle) {
    b.putInt("id", 42)
    val id: String = b.unsafeGet("id")   // CCE here, at the call site, not inside unsafeGet
}

// Safer: reified + safe cast, check happens where the type is known
inline fun <reified T> Bundle.getTyped(key: String): T? = get(key) as? T

// For collections: validate elements instead of trusting a cast
fun Any?.asStringList(): List<String>? =
    (this as? List<*>)?.takeIf { l -> l.all { it is String } }?.map { it as String }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Silencing UNCHECKED_CAST without validating. That just moves the crash to another place.
  • Believing reified checks generic arguments (List<String>). It checks only the outer class.
  • Using as T in a "convenience" helper that is used across the codebase, which spreads heap pollution everywhere.
  • Treating the CCE stack trace as the root cause and patching the read site with as?.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Bundle.get(String) deprecation matter here? → Since API 33 the untyped getters (getParcelable(key), getSerializable(key)) are deprecated in favour of class-taking overloads (getParcelable(key, Foo::class.java)). The typed overloads let the framework check the class itself. Use BundleCompat for older API levels.
  2. How do you find the original bad cast? → Search for UNCHECKED_CAST suppressions and as T helpers on the value's path. Add a temporary eager check (require(list.all { it is String })) at the suspected cast and see if the crash moves.
  3. Can Kotlin warn you at the call site? → Only at the cast. With -Werror / allWarningsAsErrors, unchecked casts must be suppressed explicitly, so every suppression gets reviewed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer says "as throws if wrong". A senior answer explains erasure-driven deferred failure, where checkcast actually gets inserted, why the stack trace misleads, and gives a policy for suppressions plus reified/element validation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A generic SavedStateHandle wrapper with as T caused ClassCastException reports in an adapter two screens away. The root cause was a key reused with a different type after a refactor.

questions.contextHtml:
The profile screen used to be an Activity. It was migrated into a @AndroidEntryPoint Fragment inside MainActivity. The custom view below hasn't changed in 2 years. The day after release, the ClassCastException rate jumps from ~0 to 1.2% of profile-screen opens, on all OS versions. Pixel and Samsung devices are equally affected. The Compose-based settings screen, which uses a similar helper, shows a smaller but non-zero number of the same crash.

class AvatarView(context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet?) : FrameLayout(context, attrs) {
    private val host = context as AppCompatActivity

    init {
        setOnClickListener {
            host.supportFragmentManager.beginTransaction()
                .add(AvatarPickerDialog(), "picker").commit()
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun ShareButton() {
    val activity = LocalContext.current as Activity
    Button(onClick = { activity.startActivity(shareIntent()) }) { Text("Share") }
}
java.lang.ClassCastException: dagger.hilt.android.internal.managers.ViewComponentManager$FragmentContextWrapper
    cannot be cast to androidx.appcompat.app.AppCompatActivity
    at com.app.profile.AvatarView.<init>(AvatarView.kt:3)
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs, explain why they only showed up now, and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Change as to as?". The view then silently does nothing on tap. Or "pass the Activity into the view's constructor", which breaks XML inflation and the layout preview.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the fragment newly annotated with @AndroidEntryPoint? Does the 1.2% equal "profile opened from the new fragment entry point"? Where is ShareButton hosted: inside a Dialog, a ContextThemeWrapper, or a Hilt fragment's ComposeView?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the cast with a context-unwrapping helper (below). If a feature flag still routes to the old Activity, flip it back for affected users in the meantime.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Context is a wrapper, not the Activity. A View's context is whatever context inflated it. Hilt @AndroidEntryPoint fragments return a FragmentContextWrapper from getContext(), and their LayoutInflater uses it, so every view inflated in that fragment has the wrapper as its context. Under the old Activity host, context really was the Activity, which is why the cast "worked" for 2 years.
    2. In Compose, LocalContext.current is the context of the hosting ComposeView. In a Hilt fragment it's the same wrapper. Inside a Dialog or under a themed wrapper it can be a ContextThemeWrapper. That explains the smaller number of crashes on the Compose screen.
    3. OEM-specific behaviour. This is ruled out because the crashes are evenly spread across manufacturers.
  4. How I'd verify each: In the debugger, check context.javaClass inside AvatarView.<init>. Walk (context as ContextWrapper).baseContext until you reach the Activity. Check the Crashlytics breadcrumbs for which host the crashing screen had.
  5. Root cause: Two unsafe casts that assumed Context is an Activity. The Android contract never promised that. A Context handed to a View or composable may be any ContextWrapper chain whose base eventually is the Activity.
  6. Fix: 
    tailrec fun Context.findActivity(): Activity? = when (this) {
    is Activity -> this
    is ContextWrapper -> baseContext.findActivity()
    else -> null
}

class AvatarView(context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet?) : FrameLayout(context, attrs) {
    init {
        setOnClickListener {
            // Prefer the owning FragmentManager over reaching for the Activity at all
            val fm = findFragment<Fragment>().childFragmentManager   // androidx.fragment.app.findFragment
            AvatarPickerDialog().show(fm, "picker")
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun ShareButton() {
    val context = LocalContext.current
    Button(onClick = { context.startActivity(shareIntent()) }) { Text("Share") }  // any Context can start an Activity (add FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK only for non-Activity contexts)
}
    Also: I resolve the host on click, not in the constructor. Holding host in a field caches a strong Activity reference in a View that might be retained. Long-term, use the Activity Result API or a callback/event to the ViewModel instead of the View driving fragment transactions itself.
  7. Prevention: Add a lint rule (a custom Detector, or a detekt ForbiddenMethodCall/regex rule) that flags context as Activity, context as AppCompatActivity and LocalContext.current as. Add a UI test that hosts the view inside a Hilt fragment.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't use as? without a fallback, because that's silent breakage. I wouldn't use findActivity()!!: you can still get null from an Application context, for example in a widget or a Service-inflated view.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why does Hilt wrap the context at all?" → So that views inflated in the fragment can get Hilt's View component, scoped to that fragment (@WithFragmentBindings).
  • "Is findFragment() safe in init?" → No. The view isn't attached yet, so findFragment throws IllegalStateException. That's why I call it in the click handler.
  • "Does a tailrec here matter?" → Wrapper chains are a few levels deep. tailrec is a free guarantee against deep recursion, not a performance requirement.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: During a "move screens to single-activity" migration, a team found 14 context as XActivity casts with one grep. Fixing them all ahead of the move avoided a week of crash firefighting.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Changes as to as?, or adds try/catch.
  • Hire: Explains ContextWrapper and the Hilt FragmentContextWrapper, and writes the findActivity() unwrap loop.
  • Strong hire: Also explains the Compose LocalContext variant, avoids caching the Activity in the view, avoids findFragment in init, and adds a lint rule plus a hosted test.

questions.promptHtml: Kotlin has no separate int and Integer. So how does Kotlin decide whether an Int is a JVM primitive or a boxed object, and why should you care?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you understand that Kotlin's unified type system still compiles to primitives and boxes. Boxing has real allocation and equality consequences.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin's Int becomes a JVM int wherever it can. It gets boxed into java.lang.Integer when it has to be an object: when it's nullable (Int?), when it's used as a generic type argument (List<Int>, Map<String, Int>, T), when it's passed as Any, or when it goes into a non-reified generic. Boxing costs an allocation, except for cached small values, and an unboxing read. It also makes identity comparison (===) unreliable. For hot paths and large arrays I use non-null Int and IntArray.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Kotlin declaration JVM representation
val a: Int = 5 int
val b: Int? = 5 Integer (Integer.valueOf(5))
val c: List<Int> List<Integer>
val d: Array<Int> Integer[]
val e: IntArray int[]
fun <T> id(t: T) called with 5 boxed
val f: Any = 5 boxed
val g: Comparable<Int> = 5 boxed

Mechanics:

  • Boxing calls Integer.valueOf(i), which returns a cached instance for -128..127 and allocates a new one otherwise. Unboxing calls intValue(), and unboxing a null throws NPE. Kotlin only unboxes after a null check or !!, so the NPE shows up at the !! or at the Java boundary.
  • Arithmetic on Int? needs a null check first. After a smart cast, Kotlin unboxes, computes on int, and re-boxes if you store the result back in an Int?.
  • Lambdas: (Int) -> Int as a Function1 boxes its arguments and return value, because Function1<P, R> is generic. Inline higher-order functions avoid this.

Cost on Android: an Integer object is about 16 bytes, versus 4 bytes for an int. Boxing 1M values in a loop means 1M short-lived allocations, which creates GC pressure and frame-time jitter on low-end devices.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun sumBoxed(xs: List<Int>): Int {         // each element is an Integer
    var s = 0
    for (x in xs) s += x                    // unbox per element
    return s
}

fun sumPrimitive(xs: IntArray): Int {       // int[]; no boxing
    var s = 0
    for (x in xs) s += x
    return s
}

var maybe: Int? = null
fun inc() { maybe = (maybe ?: 0) + 1 }      // unbox, add, Integer.valueOf (allocates when > 127)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Int? for "maybe loaded" counters in hot code, which boxes on every write.
  • Using Array<Int> when IntArray was intended. They look alike but have very different memory costs.
  • Using a HashMap<Int, V> with millions of keys. Every key is boxed. Android's SparseArray/SparseIntArray, or a primitive collection, avoids this.
  • Assuming === on Int? compares values (next question).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does listOf(1, 2, 3).sum() box? → The list stores Integers, so it unboxes each one. The values 1..3 come from the cache, so no allocation happens there.
  2. How do value classes behave here? → A @JvmInline value class UserId(val v: Int) is stored as int when used as its own type. It is boxed when nullable, generic or passed as Any, by the same rules (see the value-class section).
  3. How would you prove boxing is your problem? → Use an Android Studio Memory Profiler allocation recording, filtered to java.lang.Integer, or a Perfetto heap profile. Then look at the decompiled bytecode for Integer.valueOf calls.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer says "Int? is boxed". A senior answer lists every boxing trigger (nullable, generics, Any, Function types), quantifies the memory difference, and names primitive alternatives (IntArray, SparseIntArray, inline HOFs).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chart library stored samples in List<Float>. Switching to FloatArray cut allocations during pinch-zoom from ~200k/s to near zero, and the frame drops on low-end devices went away.

questions.promptHtml: Why does val a: Int? = 127; val b: Int? = 127; a === b print true, while the same code with 128 prints false?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the classic boxing gotcha. They want the mechanism (Integer.valueOf cache), not "Kotlin is weird".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Int? values are boxed through Integer.valueOf, and the JDK keeps a cache of Integer objects for -128 to 127. So two boxings of 127 return the same object and === (reference identity) is true. 128 is outside the cache, so each boxing allocates a new object and === is false, even though == is true. == in Kotlin calls equals, which is what you want for values. === on numbers is almost always a bug.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• == on Int? compiles to Intrinsics.areEqual(a, b): if a is null it checks b == null, otherwise it calls a.equals(b). It compares values and is null-safe.
  • === compiles to the JVM reference comparison (if_acmpne).
  • Integer.valueOf(int) returns a cached object for -128..127. That range is required by the Java language specification for boxing conversions. HotSpot can extend the upper bound with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax, but that is a HotSpot-only knob and has no equivalent on ART. Never rely on it.
  • The same caching applies to Long.valueOf, Short.valueOf and Byte.valueOf (-128..127), and to Character.valueOf (0..127). Boolean.valueOf returns one of two singletons. Float/Double have no cache.
  • For non-null Int, === compares primitives by value. Recent Kotlin compilers report identity equality on primitive and number types as deprecated or warning-level, because the result depends on boxing. The exact diagnostic differs between K1 and K2. Treat the warning as an error.
a: Int? = 127 ─┐
               ├─> Integer.valueOf(127) ─> [cached Integer@1] ── a === b  true
b: Int? = 127 ─┘

a: Int? = 128 ──> Integer.valueOf(128) ─> new Integer@7 ─┐
b: Int? = 128 ──> Integer.valueOf(128) ─> new Integer@9 ─┴─ a === b  false, a == b  true

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun main() {
    val x = 128
    val a: Int? = x
    val b: Int? = x
    println(a == b)    // true  (equals)
    println(a === b)   // false (different Integer objects)

    val c: Long? = 100L
    val d: Long? = 100L
    println(c === d)   // true, but only because 100 is in Long's cache, so don't rely on it
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing tests with small IDs (1, 2, 3). Identity comparisons pass, and production IDs in the thousands fail.
  • Comparing Long? timestamps or IDs from Room nullable columns with ===.
  • Thinking == on boxed numbers of different types compares values. Int? and Long? with the same value are not equals (Integer.equals(Long) is false). Kotlin rejects == between Int and Long at compile time for non-null numeric types, but through Any or generics the comparison just returns false.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a == b cost more than ===? → One virtual equals call. That's negligible. Correctness wins.
  2. What about data class equals with Int? fields? → Generated equals uses Intrinsics.areEqual per property, so it compares values and is safe.
  3. Where else does the cache bite? → Using boxed numbers as locks (synchronized(count)) shares the lock with every other user of that cached object in the process. Never lock on boxed values.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer says "use == not ===". A senior answer explains Integer.valueOf caching, the JLS range, that AutoBoxCacheMax is HotSpot-only, the cross-type equals trap, and the shared-lock hazard.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A selection-state bug passed QA on a seeded database with 20 items and broke for every user whose item IDs were above 127. The full story is in the next scenario.

questions.contextHtml:
A notes app has 600k DAU and a RecyclerView with a ListAdapter. After release 3.8, users report "the whole list flashes on every edit", "scroll jumps to top", and "the swipe animation is gone". Play Console shows slow frames rising from 4% to 19% on the notes list, but only for long-time users. New users and QA, who use seeded DBs with about 30 notes, see nothing. The release also updated RecyclerView 1.3.1 → 1.3.2 and enabled R8 full mode. The diff in the adapter:

@Entity data class NoteEntity(@PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Long? = null, val title: String, val updatedAt: Long)

object NoteDiff : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<NoteEntity>() {
    override fun areItemsTheSame(old: NoteEntity, new: NoteEntity) = old.id === new.id   // changed from == in 3.8 "for speed"
    override fun areContentsTheSame(old: NoteEntity, new: NoteEntity) = old == new
}

Perfetto on an affected device shows RV OnBindView for every visible row on each submitList, instead of one row.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how you'd diagnose and fix this, and what you'd put in place so it can't recur.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "RecyclerView update regression, roll it back", or "R8 full mode broke DiffUtil". Both are red herrings that waste a release cycle. Or: "add setHasStableIds(true)", which treats the symptom without understanding it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does the effect correlate with note count or note ID values? Long-time users have large auto-increment IDs.
    • Exactly what changed in the adapter between 3.7 and 3.8?
    • Is the flashing also present in a debug build? That would rule R8 in or out.
    • Can we get a DB export from an affected beta user?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the one-line === → == change in a hotfix. It's low risk, and the change was made "for speed", which there's no evidence for.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Boxed identity comparison. id is Long?, so each NoteEntity holds a java.lang.Long. Room creates a fresh Long per row per query with Long.valueOf, which is cached only for -128..127. Old and new lists come from different queries, so for IDs above 127 old.id === new.id is false. DiffUtil decides every item was removed and re-inserted: a full rebind, lost item animations, and the scroll position isn't preserved. For IDs at or below 127 the cache makes it "work", which is exactly the QA dataset.
    2. RecyclerView 1.3.2 regression. Unlikely, because the symptom depends on user data, and DiffUtil logic didn't change in a way that would cause this.
    3. R8 full mode changing equals. R8 doesn't change === semantics. It can be checked quickly with a debug build.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Unit test: NoteDiff.areItemsTheSame(note(id = 200), note(id = 200)) with separately boxed Longs returns false. This reproduces it in seconds.
    • Seed a debug DB with IDs starting at 1000 (INSERT ... id = 1000) and watch the flash in a debug build. That rules out R8.
    • Perfetto/systrace: count onBindViewHolder calls per submitList before and after the fix.
    • Revert RecyclerView only and confirm there's no change.
  5. Root cause: Reference identity on boxed Long? values. Each Room row creates new Long objects, and the JDK box cache only covers -128..127, so identity matches only for small IDs.
  6. Fix: 
    override fun areItemsTheSame(old: NoteEntity, new: NoteEntity) = old.id == new.id
    Long-term: make IDs non-null in the domain or UI model (val id: Long), mapped from the entity after insert. That keeps it a primitive long and removes the nullable sentinel. Optionally, a @JvmInline value class NoteId(val raw: Long) gives type safety. As a non-null property type it stays unboxed in the class field. It does get boxed as a generic argument, but == stays correct either way.
  7. Prevention:
    • Enable allWarningsAsErrors for the module, or at least make identity-equality warnings on numeric types errors.
    • Add a detekt/custom lint rule that bans === where either operand is a boxed number or String.
    • Make test fixtures use realistic IDs (start at 10_000).
    • Track a "full-rebind" metric: count onBindViewHolder calls per submitList in debug builds, or watch the slow-frame metric per screen in Play Console and JankStats.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't add setHasStableIds(true) as the fix. It's orthogonal to ListAdapter diffing and hides the bug. I wouldn't roll back RecyclerView or R8 "just in case": two unnecessary rollbacks cost a release train and teach the team nothing. === was never faster in a way that matters. A boxed equals call is nanoseconds per item.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "What if the ID were String?" → Room creates new String objects per row, and === fails for every item, regardless of value. Interning is unreliable as a fix. Use ==.
  • "Would Long (non-null) have had this bug?" → No. === on primitive long compares values, and modern compilers warn that it's pointless or deprecated. The nullable type is what forced the boxing.
  • "How would you prove the slow-frame drop was caused by this and not by an unrelated change?" → Stage the hotfix rollout at 10% and compare that cohort's slow-frame rate on the notes screen in Play Console vitals and JankStats against the remaining 90%.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "micro-optimization" pass replaced == with === in a handful of places. One of them was a payment-method selection check, which failed only for users with more than 127 saved methods in their history. The bug was found months later through support tickets, not through any metric.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Chases RecyclerView/R8, or suggests notifyDataSetChanged/stable IDs without finding the comparison.
  • Hire: Spots === on Long?, explains the -128..127 cache and why QA missed it, fixes with ==, and adds a unit test.
  • Strong hire: All of the above, plus explains Room's per-row object creation and DiffUtil's remove-and-insert behaviour, rules out the red herrings with cheap experiments, moves to non-null IDs, and adds lint, realistic fixtures and a staged-rollout check.

questions.promptHtml: Kotlin won't let you assign an Int to a Long variable. Why not, and what are the rules for numeric conversions, literals, and mixed arithmetic?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Java developers expect implicit widening. This checks you know Kotlin's explicit model and its edge cases (literals, narrowing, truncation).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In Kotlin, numeric types aren't subtypes of each other. Int isn't a Long, so there's no implicit widening on assignment or argument passing. You convert explicitly with toLong(), toInt(), toDouble() and so on. Literals are the exception: an integer literal takes the expected type if it fits (val l: Long = 5), and it defaults to Int, or to Long if it's too big for Int. Arithmetic between mixed types is allowed through operator overloads and returns the wider type (Int + Long → Long). Narrowing conversions silently truncate or wrap, and Double.toInt() truncates toward zero and saturates.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why no implicit widening: if Int were a subtype of Long, then val i: Int? = 1; val l: Long? = i would make a boxed Integer pose as a Long, and l == 1L would be false (Integer.equals(Long)). Kotlin avoids that whole class of bugs by requiring explicit conversion.

Rules:

Situation Behaviour
val x = 1 Int
val x = 3_000_000_000 Long (doesn't fit Int)
val x: Long = 1 OK, the literal adapts
val x: Byte = 300 Compile error (out of range)
val x = 1L, 1.0, 1f, 0xFF, 0b1010, 1_000 Long, Double, Float, Int, Int, Int
val i = 1; val l: Long = i Compile error: type mismatch
fun f(l: Long); f(i) Compile error. Use f(i.toLong())
1 + 2L Long
5 / 2 2 (integer division truncates)
5 / 2.0 2.5
300.toByte() 44 (keeps the low 8 bits: 300 − 256)
130.toByte() -126
3.99.toInt() / (-3.99).toInt() 3 / -3 (toward zero)
Double.NaN.toInt() 0
1e20.toInt() Int.MAX_VALUE (saturates)
Int.MAX_VALUE + 1 Int.MIN_VALUE (silent wraparound)

Notes on newer versions: converting Double/Float directly to Byte/Short is deprecated in modern Kotlin. Go through toInt() first. Char is not a number: Char.toInt() was deprecated in 1.5 in favour of .code, and generic Number.toChar() is deprecated in recent versions. Check the API docs for your Kotlin version before relying on these.

Unsigned types (UInt, ULong, literal 1u) also need explicit conversion and are value classes over the signed types.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val bytes: Long = 5                         // literal adapts
val count: Int = 3
// val total: Long = count                  // error: type mismatch
val total: Long = count.toLong()

val done = 3; val all = 7
val avg = 7 / 2                             // 2
val avgExact = 7 / 2.0                      // 3.5
val percent = (done * 100 / all)            // Int; fine if done*100 doesn't overflow
val ratio = done.toDouble() / all           // do the conversion BEFORE dividing

val days = 30
// val ms: Long = days * 86_400_000         // error: Int expression, no widening to Long
val msWrong: Long = (days * 86_400_000).toLong()  // compiles, but overflowed in Int first: -1702967296
val msRight: Long = days * 86_400_000L            // Int * Long -> Long: 2592000000

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• (a / b).toDouble() converts after integer division. The fraction is already gone.
  • Assuming toLong() "fixes" an overflow. (daysInt * 86_400_000).toLong() overflows in Int first (see the scenario after this).
  • Comparing Int with Long through Any: (1 as Any) == (1L as Any) is false.
  • Assuming Double.toInt() rounds. It truncates. Use roundToInt() (from kotlin.math), which throws on NaN.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you compare 1 == 1L? → For non-null numeric types the compiler rejects == between Int and Long ("Operator '==' cannot be applied"). Use 1.toLong() == 1L or compareTo, which has mixed overloads, so 1 < 2L compiles.
  2. How do you detect overflow? → Math.addExact/multiplyExact from java.lang.Math (available on Android API 24+) throw ArithmeticException. Or compute in Long and range-check.
  3. Why does 0xFFFFFFFF infer Long? → It's 4294967295, which doesn't fit Int. For ARGB colors use 0xFFFF0000.toInt().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer says "use toLong()". A senior answer explains why there's no widening (boxed equals semantics), knows the literal-typing rules, and knows the truncation, saturation and NaN behaviour. They also convert before the risky operation, not after.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A progress bar computed (downloaded / total * 100) with Ints and showed 0% until the download finished. One toFloat() placed before the division fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
You're running the post-incident review. A news app (1.5M DAU) caches article lists, and the TTL is driven by remote config cache_ttl_days (default 7). On Tuesday at 10:00 product changed it to 30 to "reduce backend load". By 10:20 the article API's QPS had gone from 2.1k to 17k (8x). The backend started returning 429s, and app-side p95 feed load went from 380 ms to 4.2 s. Rolling the config back to 7 at 11:05 restored everything. Relevant code:

fun ttlMillis(days: Int): Long = (days * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000).toLong()

fun isFresh(savedAt: Long, now: Long, days: Int) = now - savedAt < ttlMillis(days)

A unit test isFresh(savedAt = 0, now = 1000, days = 7) passes. There's also a Slack thread blaming a CDN change that went out Tuesday at 09:30.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review. What happened mechanically, why didn't tests catch it, and what changes do you commit to?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "CDN change caused it", which ignores that the config rollback fixed it. Or "toLong() is already there, so it's not overflow". Or "set a max of 7 days in remote config", which treats the symptom.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Did the QPS spike start at the config fetch time or at the CDN change? The timeline says 10:00 → 10:20, which matches config propagation.
    • What values did ttlMillis return in the field? Do we log cache decisions anywhere?
    • Are other call sites using the same helper (image cache, rate limiter)?
    • Was there any staged rollout of the config value?
  2. Immediate mitigation (already done): The config rollback. I'd add a server-side guard rail on that key right away (allowed range 1..24) until the code fix ships.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Int overflow before widening. days * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 is evaluated entirely in Int because every operand is Int. The toLong() runs after the damage is done. Max Int = 2,147,483,647 ms ≈ 24.86 days. For 30 days: 30 × 86,400,000 = 2,592,000,000, which wraps to 2,592,000,000 − 4,294,967,296 = −1,702,967,296. now - savedAt < -1.7e9 is always false, so every cache entry is stale and every screen open hits the network. That explains the 8x QPS.
    2. CDN change at 09:30. This doesn't explain a 20-minute lag, nor why a client-config rollback fixed it. It's a red herring.
    3. A thundering-herd effect from synchronized cache expiry. That would give a spike that decays, not a sustained 8x that ends exactly at rollback.
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test of ttlMillis(30) returns a negative number, which reproduces it immediately. The backend QPS graph lines up with the config fetch timestamps from the remote-config fetch logs. CDN logs show the origin-request ratio unchanged before 10:00.
  5. Root cause: Arithmetic done in a type too narrow for the result, with an explicit widening applied after the overflow. Kotlin's lack of implicit widening made it look safe, because there's a toLong() right there. The tests only exercised values whose products fit in Int (7 days = 604,800,000 ms).
  6. Fix: 
    import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.days

// Short-term: widen the first operand so the whole chain is Long
fun ttlMillis(days: Int): Long = days * 24L * 60 * 60 * 1000

// Long-term: no hand-rolled time math; use kotlin.time (stable since Kotlin 1.6)
fun ttl(days: Int) = days.coerceIn(1, 90).days
fun isFresh(savedAt: Long, now: Long, days: Int) = (now - savedAt) < ttl(days).inWholeMilliseconds
    TimeUnit.DAYS.toMillis(days.toLong()) is an acceptable alternative on Java-flavoured codebases. Clamping (coerceIn) protects against hostile or mistaken config values.
  7. Prevention:
    • Add tests at boundaries: 24, 25, 30, 365 days, and Int.MAX_VALUE. Property-based tests that assert ttlMillis(d) > 0 for every d in the valid range are cheap here.
    • Validate remote config: a typed schema with ranges both on the server and on the client (clamp and log a non-fatal when out of range).
    • Roll out config changes in stages, with automatic rollback when backend QPS or app error-rate alarms trip.
    • Add a lint/detekt rule (or a review checklist item) that flags * 1000 or * 60 chains on Int that are later converted with toLong(). Banning hand-rolled millisecond arithmetic in favour of Duration is the cleaner policy.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't just cap the config at 7, because that leaves the bug for the next caller. I wouldn't blame the CDN team without evidence: the timeline and the rollback point to the config change. I wouldn't use Math.multiplyExact everywhere, since Duration removes the class of bug instead of crashing on it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why didn't the compiler catch it?" → The compiler can warn about overflow only in constant expressions it evaluates itself, such as all-literal arithmetic. With a runtime days value it can't know the result, and Kotlin integer arithmetic wraps silently at runtime, just like Java.
  • "Could Long math overflow too?" → Not for realistic durations: Long ms covers about 292 million years. Nanosecond math overflows after about 292 years, which matters for System.nanoTime deltas only if you do something weird.
  • "How much backend cost did this incur?" → Roughly 15k extra QPS for 65 minutes ≈ 58M extra requests. That gets priced with the backend team and goes in the review.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A daily "rate the app" throttle used days * 86_400_000 in Int. When marketing set it to 60 days, every user got prompted on every launch for a weekend, and ratings dropped. The fix was a one-character L, and the lesson was to use typed config with range validation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Doesn't identify the overflow, or thinks toLong() prevents it.
  • Hire: Computes the overflow (≈24.8-day threshold, negative TTL), explains why every entry became stale, fixes with Long or Duration, and adds boundary tests.
  • Strong hire: All of the above, plus dismisses the red herrings with timeline evidence, adds config validation and staged rollout with auto-rollback, quantifies the impact, and proposes systemic prevention (ban manual ms math).

questions.promptHtml: What is a Char in Kotlin, how are Strings represented, and what do string templates and raw strings compile to? Where do they bite you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Text handling causes real bugs: Unicode, "null" in the UI, locale issues, allocation in loops. This question shows whether you know the representation or just the syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On the JVM a Char is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit. It is not a number: you get its code with .code and a digit's value with digitToInt(). A String is an immutable java.lang.String, and its API is in UTF-16 units, so length counts code units, not user-visible characters. String templates ("$a ${b.c}") compile to concatenation, either a StringBuilder chain or invokedynamic string concat when the JVM target is 9+, which D8 desugars on Android. They call toString() on each value, so a null prints as "null". Raw strings ("""...""") have no escape sequences and keep newlines. $ still interpolates, so you write ${'$'} for a literal dollar sign, and you normally finish with trimIndent() or trimMargin().

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Char

  • Char is not a subtype of Number, unlike Java's char, which is an integer type. 'a' + 1 gives 'b' (Char + Int → Char), and 'c' - 'a' gives 2 (Char − Char → Int). Char.toInt() was deprecated in Kotlin 1.5. Use .code, Char(code), digitToInt() and digitToIntOrNull().
  • A nullable Char? is boxed to Character, and the cache covers 0..127.
  • A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, such as most emoji, takes two Chars (a surrogate pair). Some user-perceived characters are several code points joined together (ZWJ sequences, flags, skin tones). See the next scenario.

String

  • Immutable, with value equality through ==. Literals are interned in the constant pool, so "a" === "a" is usually true, but strings built at runtime are not interned. Never use === on strings.
  • Storage is an implementation detail. Recent ART versions store Latin-1-only strings in a compressed 8-bit form, but the API always behaves as UTF-16.
  • s[i], substring, take and length all work in UTF-16 units. codePointAt and codePointCount work in code points. Grapheme clusters need BreakIterator.

Templates

  • "Hi $name, you have ${items.size} items" compiles to StringBuilder().append("Hi ").append(name)...toString(). Kotlin 1.5.20+ emits invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants when targeting JVM 9+, and Android's D8/R8 desugar that back into builder code. Either way, each evaluation allocates.
  • Values go through String.valueOf, so null becomes "null" and objects use toString(). A data class's toString() includes every property, which can leak PII into logs.
  • Inside a loop, use buildString {} or joinToString instead of += on a String, which costs O(n²) in copies.

Raw strings

  • """ has no escape processing (\n stays as two characters) and keeps literal newlines and indentation.
  • trimIndent() removes the common minimal indent and the first and last blank lines. trimMargin("|") strips everything up to and including the margin prefix.
  • $ still starts a template, so a literal $ before an identifier needs ${'$'}. Kotlin 2.x adds multi-dollar interpolation ($$"""...""") for this. Check its stability status for your version; it's covered in the Kotlin 2.x features section.

Formatting

  • "%.2f".format(x) uses the default locale, so in de-DE it produces 3,14. For machine-readable output (JSON by hand, analytics keys, SQL), pass Locale.ROOT: String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%.2f", x).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val user: User? = null
textView.text = "Hello $user"                 // shows "Hello null" in production UI
textView.text = "Hello ${user?.name ?: getString(R.string.guest)}"

val digit = '7'.digitToInt()                  // 7, not 55
val code = 'A'.code                           // 65

val query = """
    SELECT * FROM notes
    WHERE price > ${'$'}minPrice              
    AND title LIKE '%\n%'                     
""".trimIndent()                              // ${'$'} gives a literal $; \n here is backslash + n, not a newline

val csv = buildString {                       // one builder, not O(n^2) concatenation
    rows.forEach { append(it.id).append(',').append(it.name).append('\n') }
}

val price = String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%.2f", 3.14159)   // "3.14" regardless of device locale

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using "$nullable" in UI text, which prints "null" with no compile error.
  • Using '7'.code (55) where digitToInt() (7) was meant. In Java, c - '0' habits carry over unsafely.
  • Assuming length equals visible characters, then truncating with take(n) and splitting an emoji.
  • Writing \n in a raw string and expecting a newline, or forgetting that $ interpolates inside raw strings in regex and SQL.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is "a" + "b" concatenated at compile time? → Yes. Constant expressions are folded, and const val strings are inlined into callers (see the const val question in the properties section).
  2. Does trimIndent() run at runtime? → It's a stdlib function, so semantically yes. The Kotlin JVM compiler can fold it for compile-time-constant raw strings in recent versions. Check the bytecode if it matters in a hot path. It rarely does.
  3. Why is == on strings safe but === misleading in tests? → Literal interning makes === pass for constants and fail for runtime-built strings, such as those parsed from JSON or read from a DB.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer knows the syntax. A senior answer knows that Char is a UTF-16 unit and not a number, what templates compile to and allocate, how null and toString leak into UI and logs, the $ rules in raw strings, and the locale trap in format.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A price string built with "%.2f".format(...) was sent to a payments API. Users with a German locale sent "9,99", and the backend rejected it. The fix was Locale.ROOT, plus a typed decimal in the request model.

questions.contextHtml:
A chat app (900k DAU, 40% of users in markets where emoji-heavy names are common) has the product spec "Display name: max 20 characters. Notification preview: first 40 characters + ellipsis." The current code:

fun isValidName(name: String) = name.isNotBlank() && name.length <= 20
fun preview(body: String) = if (body.length > 40) body.take(40) + "…" else body

Support tickets: (a) "App says my name is too long but it's only 6 flags" (each flag is 2 code points = 4 UTF-16 units, so 6 flags = 24 units). (b) The iOS app accepts the same name. (c) Notification previews sometimes end with a box or a ? before the ellipsis. (d) The backend rejected about 0.2% of profile updates with 400 invalid UTF-8 after the client started doing name.toByteArray() for a signature. The backend column is VARCHAR(20) with utf8mb4 (counts code points). A red herring in the Slack thread: "it's the font on Samsung devices".
questions.promptHtml: What does "20 characters" mean, and how would you implement validation and truncation correctly across clients and backend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use codePointCount instead of length." That fixes some cases, but flags, ZWJ families and skin tones are still split or miscounted. It also doesn't address the cross-platform contract or the backend limit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is "character" what the user perceives (grapheme clusters)? That's what iOS String.count counts, which explains (b).
    • What's the backend's real limit: code points (utf8mb4 VARCHAR(20)), bytes (an index or column limit), or both?
    • Is the preview length a UI-space concern (and should it be done by TextView ellipsizing), or a payload-size concern (bytes, for FCM's 4 KB data limit)?
    • Do we need to normalize (NFC) before counting, since "é" can be 1 or 2 code points?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Relax the client name check so it isn't stricter than the backend: count code points, which matches VARCHAR(20) utf8mb4. Make preview surrogate-safe. Both are low-risk hotfixes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. UTF-16 unit counting. length counts Chars. One flag = 2 code points = 4 units, and one family emoji (man ZWJ woman ZWJ girl) = 5 code points = 8 units = 1 grapheme. That explains (a) and (b).
    2. Splitting a surrogate pair. take(40) can cut between a high and a low surrogate and leave a lone surrogate. Renderers draw a replacement glyph, which explains (c). String.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8) replaces unmappable lone surrogates with ? (0x3F), so the signature is computed over different bytes than the server sees. That explains (d).
    3. Samsung fonts. Ruled out because it reproduces on Pixel with the same strings. It's the red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: Write unit tests with explicit escapes: flag "🇮🇳" (2 code points, 4 units), family "👨‍👩‍👧" (8 units). Assert length, codePointCount(0, length) and the grapheme count. Run preview() across a fuzzed corpus and assert that no result contains an unpaired surrogate (Character.isHighSurrogate(last)).
  5. Root cause: An ambiguous spec ("characters") was implemented with the cheapest unit (UTF-16 code units), while iOS used graphemes and the backend used code points. On top of that, truncation was done at unit boundaries.
  6. Fix: Agree on a contract, and write it down:
    • User-facing limits = grapheme clusters (matches iOS and user expectations).
    • Storage limit = code points or bytes, enforced by the backend. The client also checks it as a secondary rule, so that "fits in 20 graphemes but exceeds 20 code points" (e.g. 3 families = 15 code points, fine; 5 families = 25 code points) gets a clear message. Alternatively, widen the column, which is usually the right call.
    import android.icu.text.BreakIterator   // API 24+; ICU data is updated with the OS

fun String.graphemeCount(): Int {
    val it = BreakIterator.getCharacterInstance().also { b -> b.setText(this) }
    var n = 0
    while (it.next() != BreakIterator.DONE) n++
    return n
}

fun String.takeGraphemes(max: Int): String {
    val it = BreakIterator.getCharacterInstance().also { b -> b.setText(this) }
    var end = 0
    repeat(max) {
        val next = it.next()
        if (next == BreakIterator.DONE) return this
        end = next
    }
    return substring(0, end)
}

fun isValidName(name: String) =
    name.isNotBlank() && name.graphemeCount() <= 20 && name.codePointCount(0, name.length) <= 20

fun preview(body: String): String {
    val cut = body.takeGraphemes(40)
    return if (cut.length < body.length) "$cut…" else body
}
    • For on-screen previews, prefer TextView maxLines + ellipsize, or Compose maxLines + TextOverflow.Ellipsis. The text engine truncates at visual and grapheme boundaries and adapts to width, which beats a fixed count.
    • Normalize with java.text.Normalizer.normalize(name, Normalizer.Form.NFC) before validating and storing, so the same name always counts the same.
  7. Prevention: Put a shared spec in the API contract ("limits are in grapheme clusters; server limit is N code points"). Keep a golden test corpus shared with iOS and backend (flags, ZWJ, skin tones, combining marks, RTL). Add a lint/detekt rule against take(/substring( on user-generated text in UI layers. For EditText, note that InputFilter.LengthFilter counts UTF-16 units (it avoids splitting surrogate pairs, but still counts units), so add a grapheme-aware filter.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: BreakIterator costs more than length. That doesn't matter at 20–40 graphemes, but don't run it per frame in a hot list. Cache the results. I wouldn't strip emoji or "sanitize to ASCII", which is user-hostile. I wouldn't just use codePointCount and call it done: ZWJ sequences still split, and iOS still disagrees.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why does BreakIterator on older devices give different counts?" → Its grapheme rules come from the ICU/Unicode version bundled with the OS. New emoji sequences may be counted as several clusters on old Android versions. The server should be the source of truth for hard limits, and clients should be lenient.
  • "FCM payload is limited in bytes. How does that change things?" → Truncate by UTF-8 byte budget at a grapheme boundary: walk the graphemes and accumulate toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8).size until the next grapheme would exceed the budget.
  • "Is java.text.BreakIterator enough?" → It works on all API levels. android.icu.text.BreakIterator (API 24+) uses newer ICU rules and handles modern emoji sequences better.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" emoji names with codePointCount, then got a new wave of tickets from users with skin-tone emoji, which are 2 code points each. A shared grapheme contract and a cross-platform golden corpus ended a bug class that had resurfaced every few releases.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Says "length is characters". Blames fonts. Suggests limiting to ASCII.
  • Hire: Distinguishes UTF-16 units, code points and graphemes. Fixes surrogate splitting. Uses BreakIterator.
  • Strong hire: All of the above, plus pins down the ambiguous requirement as a cross-platform contract, aligns the client with the backend storage limits, prefers text-engine ellipsizing for display, normalizes, explains the toByteArray ? replacement behind the signature errors, and adds shared golden tests.

questions.promptHtml: Where does Kotlin's type inference fail, or infer a type you didn't want? When do you choose to write explicit types even though inference would work?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers know that inference is a convenience with sharp edges, especially for public API, sealed state and mutable types. This question shows whether you've hit those edges.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Inference fails outright in a few places: recursive functions with expression bodies, lambdas without an expected type ({ x -> x * 2 }), and empty generic factories (emptyList() with nothing to infer from). The more dangerous cases are when it succeeds with the wrong type. var state = UiState.Loading infers the Loading subtype, so you can never assign Success. val state = MutableStateFlow(UiState.Loading) infers MutableStateFlow<UiState.Loading>. if (c) 1 else "x" infers an intersection type. Public members with inferred types leak implementation types (MutableStateFlow, ArrayList, RepoImpl) into your API.
