So I write explicit types on public or protected API, on sealed-state holders, and wherever the declared type should be wider than the initializer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Kotlin infers a declaration's type from its initializer's most specific type, not from how you use it later.

Case Result
fun fact(n: Int) = if (n <= 1) 1 else n * fact(n - 1) Error: type checking has run into a recursive problem. Declare : Int
val f = { x -> x * 2 } Error: cannot infer a type for parameter x
val f: (Int) -> Int = { x -> x * 2 } OK, the expected type drives the lambda
val xs = emptyList() Error: not enough information to infer type variable T
val n = null Nothing?, which is useless as a variable
var s = UiState.Loading (object subtype) UiState.Loading, so s = UiState.Success(..) is a type mismatch
val flow = MutableStateFlow(UiState.Loading) MutableStateFlow<UiState.Loading>, a compile error on the first value = Success
val v = if (c) 1 else "x" Intersection like Comparable<*> & java.io.Serializable, displayed oddly and effectively Any
var total = 0 then total += size.toLong() Error: total is Int
val name = javaUser.getName() Platform type String!, with no null check until use (see the null-safety section)
buildList { add(1) } List<Int> through builder inference (stable since Kotlin 1.7, improved under K2)

Why explicit types on public API:

  • Encapsulation: val uiState = _uiState exposes MutableStateFlow to the Fragment, which can then write to it. val uiState: StateFlow<UiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow() exposes only the read-only type.
  • Binary and source compatibility: if you change an initializer from ArrayList to listOf, the inferred public return type changes, and Java callers or other modules break without you noticing. Library modules can enforce explicit types with kotlin { explicitApi() } (explicit API mode), which requires visibility modifiers and types on public declarations.
  • Compile and IDE performance: declared types cut the inference work across module boundaries. The effect is usually small, but it is noticeable in heavily generic or DSL code.
  • Reviewability: a reader of a public signature shouldn't have to read the body.

When I leave types inferred: locals, private members with obvious initializers, and lambdas whose expected type is clear. Over-annotating locals adds noise.

K2 (Kotlin 2.0) changed inference in some edge cases, generally making it more consistent. Builder-inference and smart-cast improvements are covered in the K2 section. Don't rely on version-specific inference quirks in shared code.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface UiState {
    data object Loading : UiState
    data class Success(val items: List<String>) : UiState
}

class FeedViewModel : ViewModel() {
    // Broken: inferred MutableStateFlow<UiState.Loading>
    // private val _state = MutableStateFlow(UiState.Loading)
    // _state.value = UiState.Success(emptyList())   // type mismatch

    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<UiState>(UiState.Loading)     // widen explicitly
    val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state.asStateFlow()               // explicit, read-only API type

    // Broken: leaks MutableStateFlow to the UI (anyone can write)
    // val leaky = _state
}

fun fact(n: Int): Long = if (n <= 1) 1 else n * fact(n - 1)          // recursive -> explicit return type

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• MutableStateFlow(UiState.Loading) / mutableStateOf(Loading) without a type argument. This is common in sealed-state ViewModels.
  • Public fun repo() = RepositoryImpl(...), which leaks the implementation and couples callers to it.
  • Relying on inferred intersection or Any types from mixed if/when branches. This hides a design smell: the branches should return a common sealed type.
  • Annotating every local "for clarity" until the code is unreadable, and losing refactor flexibility.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does val x: List<Int> = ArrayList() cost anything? → No. It only narrows the static type, and the runtime object is the same.
  2. What does explicit API mode enforce? → In strict mode, missing visibility modifiers and missing return/property types on public API are errors. In warning mode they're warnings. It's aimed at library modules.
  3. Why can't the compiler infer the recursive return type? → To type the body it must know fact's return type, which depends on the body. The inference engine doesn't solve that fixpoint and asks you to break the cycle.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer says "Kotlin infers types, sometimes you need to annotate". A senior answer explains initializer-driven inference, names the dangerous successes (narrow sealed subtype, leaked mutable or implementation types, intersections), and has a policy: explicit on public API and state holders, explicit API mode for libraries, inferred for locals.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared UI module exposed val events = MutableSharedFlow<Event>() through inference. A feature team emitted into it from a Fragment, and analytics fired twice for six weeks before someone noticed.

questions.contextHtml:
An e-commerce app (3M DAU, Retrofit + Gson) shipped 9.2. Two days later, a new crash group at 0.6% of sessions, all in the product-list screen, mostly from one region:

java.lang.NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: method com.shop.ui.PriceFormatter.format, parameter currency
    at com.shop.ui.PriceFormatter.format(PriceFormatter.kt:12)
    at com.shop.ui.ProductViewHolder.bind(ProductViewHolder.kt:57)
    at androidx.recyclerview.widget.RecyclerView$Adapter.onBindViewHolder(...)

The model:

data class ProductDto(
    val id: String,
    val title: String,
    val price: Long,
    val currency: String,          // non-null in Kotlin
    val badges: List<String> = emptyList()
)

Other facts: 9.2 also turned on R8 full mode (AGP 8 upgrade). The backend team says "no API changes". But the regional pricing service was migrated on the same day, and for products in a promo it omits currency. A second, rarer crash elsewhere: NullPointerException ... List.size() on a null object reference from badges, even though it has a default value.
questions.promptHtml: Explain how a non-null Kotlin property ended up null, why the crash is far from the parse, and how you'd fix it for good.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make currency nullable", which spreads ? everywhere and loses the invariant. Or "R8 broke it, add -keep", which doesn't explain the regional pattern. Or "wrap bind in try/catch".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Can we capture a raw failing response? An OkHttp interceptor in a debug build, or a server log for the promo SKUs.
    • Is the crash limited to products from the migrated pricing service? A region or SKU breadcrumb would show it.
    • Do debug (non-R8) builds also crash with that payload? That separates the R8 hypothesis from the data hypothesis.
    • Does badges crash only when the JSON contains "badges": null, or also when the key is missing?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ask the backend to restore currency for promo SKUs, since that's the fastest lever and covers all app versions. Client-side, ship a hotfix that drops or patches invalid DTOs at the mapping layer (below) instead of crashing in bind.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Gson bypasses Kotlin's constructor. ProductDto has no no-arg constructor, because not all parameters have defaults. Gson's ConstructorConstructor falls back to UnsafeAllocator, which calls Unsafe.allocateInstance and creates the object without running any constructor. Then it sets fields reflectively from the JSON. A missing key leaves the field at the JVM default, which is null for references. Kotlin's null checks live on the constructor parameters and on function parameters, not on field reads. So the null sits silently inside a "non-null" String until it's passed to a Kotlin function with a parameter check (PriceFormatter.format, which runs Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter) or until it's dereferenced. That is why the crash is two layers away, inside onBindViewHolder.
    2. badges default ignored. The same mechanism: defaults are applied by the constructor, and Unsafe allocation never runs it, so badges is null when the key is missing. Even with a no-arg constructor (when all parameters have defaults), an explicit "badges": null in the JSON overwrites the default with null.
    3. R8 full mode stripping or renaming fields or constructors. This is a real risk in general. Without keep rules, all fields would come back null for every product. That doesn't match a regional 0.6%, so it's a plausible red herring, but I'd still verify keep rules.
  4. How I'd verify each: Write a unit test (on the JVM, no device): Gson().fromJson("""{"id":"1","title":"t","price":100}""", ProductDto::class.java).currency returns null despite the non-null type. Replay a captured promo payload in a debug build to confirm it's the data, not R8. Inspect R8's -printusage/-printseeds output or the APK Analyzer for ProductDto fields. Add a Crashlytics breadcrumb with the SKU source service.
  5. Root cause: A reflection-based parser that knows nothing about Kotlin's nullability or default arguments. Combined with a backend contract change (an omitted field), it produced objects that violate their declared types. The violation was detected far from the trust boundary, at the first Kotlin null check that happened to run.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: validate at the boundary. Map DTOs to domain models in the repository and drop (with a logged non-fatal) or default the invalid ones:
    // DTO tells the truth about the wire: anything can be missing
data class ProductDto(val id: String?, val title: String?, val price: Long?, val currency: String?, val badges: List<String>?)

fun ProductDto.toDomainOrNull(): Product? {
    val id = id ?: return null
    val currency = currency ?: return null.also { logNonFatal("missing currency", id) }
    return Product(id, title.orEmpty(), price ?: return null, currency, badges.orEmpty())
}
    • Long-term: move to a Kotlin-aware serializer that enforces nullability and defaults at parse time:
      • kotlinx.serialization (@Serializable): it's a compiler plugin with no reflection, defaults are applied, and a missing required field throws MissingFieldException. An explicit null for a non-null property fails decoding. coerceInputValues and explicitNulls control the edge cases. It's R8-friendly, so no fragile keep rules are needed.
      • Or Moshi with codegen (@JsonClass(generateAdapter = true) via KSP), which throws JsonDataException ("Required value 'currency' missing at $[3]"). Avoid Moshi's reflective KotlinJsonAdapterFactory on Android unless you accept the size and speed cost of kotlin-reflect.
      • Either way, decide how strict to be: failing the whole list because one item is bad is usually worse than dropping that item. A per-item lenient wrapper, or the DTO-to-domain mapping above, gives you that control.
    • If you must stay on Gson for now: recent Gson versions (2.9+) offer GsonBuilder().disableJdkUnsafe(), which makes Gson fail loudly on classes without a no-arg constructor instead of silently skipping constructors. Also make sure R8 keep rules cover the models. Recent Gson releases ship consumer rules, but verify for your version.
  7. Prevention:
    • Add contract tests against recorded backend responses (including promo, region and edge SKUs) in CI.
    • Make a schema or contract change in a backend service require a consumer notice. "No API changes" was false because the field became optional for a subset of products.
    • Add a lint/detekt rule or review checklist item: no non-null Kotlin properties on Gson-parsed classes. DTOs are either nullable or use a Kotlin-aware serializer.
    • Monitor: count dropped and invalid DTOs per endpoint as a metric, and alert on spikes. That catches the next contract drift before it turns into crashes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't make currency nullable in the domain/UI model: that pushes the problem into every screen. Nullable belongs only in the wire DTO. I wouldn't put a try/catch in bind, because it hides the issue and leaves blank rows. I wouldn't do a big-bang serializer migration in a hotfix. Migrating endpoint by endpoint behind tests is safer, since Gson and kotlinx.serialization can coexist through separate Retrofit converters per service. The order of converter factories matters.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why doesn't Kotlin check the field on read?" → Kotlin trusts its own types. It inserts null checks only at boundaries it knows about: public function parameters, platform-type assignments and !!. Checking every field read would cost performance everywhere to guard against tools that bypass the constructor.
  • "What if ProductDto had defaults for every parameter?" → The compiler then generates a no-arg constructor on the JVM. Gson uses it, so missing keys keep their defaults. Explicit JSON nulls still overwrite them, though, so non-null fields can still end up null.
  • "Room has the same risk?" → Much less. Room generates code that honours Kotlin nullability: a NULL column mapped to a non-null property fails at generation time or with a clear runtime error, depending on the query. Room doesn't use Unsafe.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One team "fixed" these NPEs by making every DTO field nullable and reusing DTOs as UI models. Six months later, the UI was full of ?: "" and they had shipped a "$null" price label. Separating the nullable wire DTO from a validated domain model fixed both problems.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Makes the field nullable everywhere or adds try/catch. Can't explain how a non-null field became null.
  • Hire: Explains Gson's Unsafe allocation skipping constructors and defaults, why the NPE appears at the first parameter check, and proposes validation at the boundary or a Kotlin-aware serializer.
  • Strong hire: All of the above, plus separates the hypotheses with cheap experiments (JVM unit test, debug build replay, R8 output), handles the explicit-null-over-default case, plans a gradual serializer migration with per-item leniency, and adds contract tests and invalid-DTO monitoring.
